title: Extra Parts
text:
These parts you may either already have, depend on where you're located for a good deal, depend on personal preference, or are optional. If you do not have any of these, you'll need to add around $500 to the total project cost.

**Note**: Make sure to go through the list below to make sure you have everything you need.

title: The PCBs
text:
The electronics of the rover consist of two boards: the brain board and the motor board. To order these boards we suggest that you order from JLCPCB, this PCB fabrication company is quite inexpensive for this board size and has good turnaround time. You'll either have to order the required minimum of 10 pieces or you can ask on the Slack group whether someone wants to put in a group order or already has some extras.
Upload the .zip files individually — one for the brain board and one for the motor board — and make sure the following settings are set:

title: The body plates
text: The body plates that attach to all sides of the body are designed to be made from laser cut acrylic, MDF, hardwood, or similar. The 2D cutout files are the `.dxf` files in the laser cut parts folder. They were designed to be around 3mm thick (1/8"). You can choose a material and cut them at your local makerspace's laser cutter or order them from an online service like Sculpteo or SendCutSend. Check the README in that folder for more details.

title: A gamepad or remote controller
text:
This is technically not a requirement, especially if you're planning on making the rover autonomous, but is highly recommended. Any USB based option should work here.

Some options are getting an XBox controller with a usb dongle or for longer range; the pricier Spektrum WS2000 with Spektrum DXs transmitter. Many alternatives exist and will work ok.

title: Standoff kit for the boards
text: You'll want these to mount the PCBs to the rover body. Many options exist here, for example this kit.

title: Wiring
text:
We recommend getting spools of 18AWG (red and black), 20AWG (white, red, black) and 22AWG wire (4 colors). The wire has to be stranded and not solid core as it will bend during operation. For each wire type, if possible, get ribbon cable where each wire is attached to another one which will help with keeping wiring clean and manageable.

To protect the cables from chafing against the sharp aluminum parts, we recommend cable sleeves.
You can also use grommets, filing down the sharp edges or burs, applying tape to the edges, or using expandable wire sleeving.

Heat shrink is a must have for keeping cables nice and snug.

Take a look at the wiring overview to get an idea of what you will be building. You'll need crimps and connectors for DuPont, Bullet, XT30, JST, and Molex styles. Crimping doesn't have a 100% success rate, so we recommend getting extras or buying a kit if you're planning on using them for other projects as well. Here are some options for each set you need:

title: Wiring (2)
text:
* A Raspberry Pi ribbon cable, e.g. from Adafruit but available in many places. While you could use header pins for this connection, the cable is the cleanest solution
* A USB-C power breakout cable if you're using a Raspberry Pi 5, e.g. from Amazon
* XT30 connectors for the power connections on the motor PCB.
 * DIY options, either:
 * 5 pairs M/F from Gobilda
 * 20 pairs M/F from Amazon
 * 1 pair M/F from Digikey
 * premade from GoBilda: 2x male leads, 2x female leads
* 6 4-pin JST connections:
 * 6x premade JST to jumper wires from GoBilda
 * JST connector kit
* 6 6-pin Molex PCI-E connections. Digikey carries a couple options. In either case, be sure to get enough for 6 connectors.
 * housings and pins
 * assemblies are sometimes available but the 16 AWG wire may be difficult to work with
* 4 3-pin DuPont and 8 4-pin DuPont connectors
 * DuPont connector kit
 * Buy precrimped wires+connectors from various sources
* 12 female 3.5mm Bullet connectors. Make sure you're getting the right size connectors and ones that come insulated.
 * GoBilda has various combinations available that you can cut/solder/crimp. They use 16AWG wire which is on the thicker side. Make sure you're getting the Female connector type.
 * Buy a DIY kit
 * The GoBilda connector pack is good quality but only has 5 female connectors so you would need 3 of them.
 * from Amazon (insulators are flimsy but ok)

title: Threadlocker
text: You will want threadlocker for several screws so that they don't unscrew themselves while driving. You can find this everywhere, for example at Gobilda. Make sure you get blue as opposed to red so it's not permanent.

title: Tools
text:
* A combination nut driver will save you time screwing and unscrewing (lock)nuts inside the body.
* You'll need 2.5mm and 3mm hex keys for the button and socket M4 screws respectively. For example Gobilda 2.5 and Gobilda 3.
* A crimping tool for Molex, JST, DuPont connectors. A regular crimping tool should be able to handle all of these without issue. While you can technically complete a crimp without a crimping tool, it often won't be as consistent or strong as with a proper crimper. Various connector sets come with a decent crimper.

title: Electrical
text:
* Voltage Regulators:
 * **1 X** 5V Regulator: Pololu
 * **1 X** 12V Regulator: Pololu
* **3 X** Roboclaw 2x7A Motor Controller Basic Micro
* **1 X** Power Measurement Unit INA260: Sold out on DigiKey, possible replacements are on Adafruit
* **1 X** PCA9685 steering servo driver Mouser
* DC power meter: Amazon. This LCD display reads out current, voltage, power, and energy, and can be put on the back where the rectangular hole is in the laser cut cover.
* batteries: many options available here. We recommend getting LiPo batteries. You'll need a battery that can provide over 14V(*), so a 4s battery works well. You can get batteries with various mAh ratings (how many milliAmperes the battery can output for 1 hour). We recommend any option over 4000mAh. Higher capacity comes at a higher cost. You can also get more than one battery and swap them out. The rover can carry them as well.
 * Zeee sells many options on Amazon
 * You'll also need a charger for the battery. Make sure it can support the battery you bought, chemistry-wise and connector-wise. For the Zeee options, this B6 Lipo Balance Charger from Amazon will work.
 * Consider getting a fireproof battery bag. LiPo batteries are extremely flammable/explosive and a fire caused by a battery is extremely difficult to put out.
 * You'll also need a way to connect your battery to the PCB via a XT30 connector (MH-FC) which depends on the battery you get. Often these come with the charger for the battery
* A Raspberry Pi 3, 4, or 5 and SD card for the operating system. For the 4 or 5, any amount of RAM should work just fine. Note that only the 5 has two full serial interfaces and thus is the only model that can connect to the motor controllers (Roboclaws) and run bluetooth at the same time.

title: Electrical (2)
text: > (*) The reason you need 14V is that the 12V regulator needs a dropout voltage on top of the output voltage in order to provide 12V. A 12V battery will not work adequately.

title: Different wheels
text:
* The wheels we previously included as the default from DollarHobbyz are $34.95 per pair of two for a total of $104.85 (excl. shipping), saving ~$135 compared to the default Wasteland wheels. They are a perfectly fine choice but require some drilling to fit to the motor hubs.
* Gobilda also sells a larger version of the Wasteland Wheel at 192mm diameter. This adds $90 total compared to the default Wasteland wheels. No drilling is required. Those wheels are bigger and wider and look like this:

| smaller Wasteland wheels | bigger Wasteland wheels |

| | |

There is a software parameter where you can easily modify the size of the wheels to account for speed differences.

text: Parts can become out of stock or discontinued in the future. title: Threadlocker
text: You will want threadlocker for several screws so that they don't unscrew themselves while driving. You can find this everywhere, for example at Gobilda. Make sure you get blue as opposed to red so it's not permanent.

title: Tools
text:
* A combination nut driver will save you time screwing and unscrewing (lock)nuts inside the body.
* You'll need 2.5mm and 3mm hex keys for the button and socket M4 screws respectively. For example Gobilda 2.5 and Gobilda 3.
* A crimping tool for Molex, JST, DuPont connectors. A regular crimping tool should be able to handle all of these without issue. While you can technically complete a crimp without a crimping tool, it often won't be as consistent or strong as with a proper crimper. Various connector sets come with a decent crimper.

title: Electrical
text:
* Voltage Regulators:
 * **1 X** 5V Regulator: Pololu
 * **1 X** 12V Regulator: Pololu
* **3 X** Roboclaw 2x7A Motor Controller Basic Micro
* **1 X** Power Measurement Unit INA260: Sold out on DigiKey, possible replacements are on Adafruit
* **1 X** PCA9685 steering servo driver Mouser
* DC power meter: Amazon. This LCD display reads out current, voltage, power, and energy, and can be put on the back where the rectangular hole is in the laser cut cover.
* batteries: many options available here. We recommend getting LiPo batteries. You'll need a battery that can provide over 14V(*), so a 4s battery works well. You can get batteries with various mAh ratings (how many milliAmperes the battery can output for 1 hour). We recommend any option over 4000mAh. Higher capacity comes at a higher cost. You can also get more than one battery and swap them out. The rover can carry them as well.
 * Zeee sells many options on Amazon
 * You'll also need a charger for the battery. Make sure it can support the battery you bought, chemistry-wise and connector-wise. For the Zeee options, this B6 Lipo Balance Charger from Amazon will work.
 * Consider getting a fireproof battery bag. LiPo batteries are extremely flammable/explosive and a fire caused by a battery is extremely difficult to put out.
 * You'll also need a way to connect your battery to the PCB via a XT30 connector (MH-FC) which depends on the battery you get. Often these come with the charger for the battery
* A Raspberry Pi 3, 4, or 5 and SD card for the operating system. For the 4 or 5, any amount of RAM should work just fine. Note that only the 5 has two full serial interfaces and thus is the only model that can connect to the motor controllers (Roboclaws) and run bluetooth at the same time.

title: Drive Motor Clamp - Mechanical over-constraint
text:
Drive Motor Clamp - Mechanical over-constraint 
## Problem 
The attachment scheme for the drive motors leads to a mechanical over-constraint.

 

Here we can see that the clamping force on the aluminum 25mm Diameter motor clamp will be over-constrained when bolting the clamp into the aluminum U-channel

 

The red arrows show the force put on the piece from the clamping screw, and green arrows show force put on by bolting to the u-channel. These force are in direct opposition, and overtime lead to one of two things:

 * The motor loosens inside the clamp and is allowed to free spin, which will tangle and eventually break your wires
 * The clamp loosens inside the u-channel and the wheel assembly becomes loose to the rest of the robot chassis

## Solution
The motor should mount on using the bolting pattern at the bottom of the motor, similar to the corner motor mounting scheme. This will alleviate this over constraint and allow all pieces to be tightened properly

title: Clamping Hub: Mechanical over-constraint
text:
Clamping Hub: Mechanical over-constraint
## Problem

There is a mechanical over-constraint imposed by the 0.25 inch clamping hub used to attach the corner wheel assemblies to the corner steering assemblies. 

 

This over-constraint is caused by the opposition of the clamping action of the clamping hub around the 1/4 inch shaft, and the bolting force attaching it to the aluminum U-channel

 

The force caused by the clamping hub is shown in red, and force from the bolting to the U-channel is shown in green. There is not enough tolerance in the clamping hub to both very tightly grip around shaft and bolt to the u-channel.

## Solution

In order to solve this issue you need to find a way to de-couple the attachment of the hub from the clamping force on the 0.25 in shaft. This could be done in many different ways, a few potential solutions would be:

 * Find a way to split this piece up into multiple pieces that are not coupled rigidly in those directions
 * Find a way to increase the mechanical tolerance in the bolting so that these forces are not in opposition

title: Shaft Coupler -
text:
Shaft Coupler - 
## Problem

There is sometimes slippage in the attachment between the shaft coupler and the motor shaft

 

(this image shows socket head cap screws, which have been switched to button head screws for more clearance) 

Even with the de-coupling of the two clamping forces across the coupler it still sometimes does not grab onto the motor shaft well enough to hold the entire torque seen on the corners. 

## Solution

In order to keep the JPL open source rover up and running I've simply epoxied the couplers to the motor shafts, however for a hobby level project where one might want to change or reuse the motors this wouldn't be ideal. 

Instead a coupler that can appropriately grab onto the 4mm motor shaft would be idea. This could potentially include a redesign of the scheme of attaching the motor so that you can get increased length of motor shaft to attach to as well.

title: Corner Encoder System - General Improvement possible
text:
Corner Encoder System - General Improvement possible
## Problem

The absolute encoders used on the corner system are relatively expensive, and also require a voltage scaling solution to convert from the 0-5V analog output signal to the 0-2V scale that the RoboClaw motor controller accepts as input.

## Solutions

There are many potential solutions to this problem, and could be an improvement in complexity, or cost. Below are a few proposed potential solutions that could be explored further. 

### Cheaper Absolute Encoders

One solution would be just using a cheaper absolute encoder, one example would be https://www.usdigital.com/products/encoders/absolute/rotary/kit/MAE3 . These would require a little bit of design work as they are to be mounted in-line with the output shaft of the motor. These are about $10 cheaper per encoder, but also allow you to skip buying the gearing system for each corner as well, meaning you save closer to $20 per corner


### Potentiometer

To greatly increase the cost savings on the system you could use a potentiometer (variable resistor) in order to do get the absolute position on the corners. This would be a bit more work on the design side to mount a pot in a correct way, as well as tune all the numbers correctly. Below is a forum thread on arduinos' site that talks about this a little bit. 

https://forum.arduino.cc/index.php?topic=262286.0

### Quadrature Encoder

Another high cost-savings solution would be to replace the entire absolute encoder system with a standard quadra

title: Helpful jig for drilling clamping hub mounting holes in Traxx wheels
text:
Helpful jig for drilling clamping hub mounting holes in Traxx wheels
When the **Houston Robotics** Mars Rover team began to address the drilling of the mounting holes in the Traxxas wheels, we pondered how we might more accurately accomplish this. Initially we considered a vertical lathed spindle 12mm at the bottom to fit the wheel and 4mm at the top to fit the hub. Rotational orientation would still be by hand and there was concern that using the hub itself as a guide may damage the threads. We consulted the **Houston Community College** Stafford manufacturing campus Fab Lab supervisor **Roland Fields**. He suggested a more modern high tech approach of creating a 3D printed jig to fit the wheel hub to include appropriately spaced holes to guide pilot hole drilling. He directed us to lab assistant **Frederic Lemme** who whipped up a prototype on SolidWorks. After tweaking for fit, a further modification adding a hex nut shape to fit into the wheel ensured fixed alignment of the pilot hole guides to the target area. **Houston Robotics'** **Omar Gomez** and son accomplished the final drilling. The screws to attach the wheel to the hub seemed excessively long, but that's an issue for further along the build. ATTACHED is a drawing of the wheel adapter and zip file of the .SLDPRT and .STL files. Copyright 2018 **Houston Robotics**, free to use with acknowledgement.

title: Logic Shifter board testing confusion - put DIR & OE to GND instead of GPIO
text:
Logic Shifter board testing confusion - put DIR & OE to GND instead of GPIO
In testing the Logic Shifter Board section 4 and Figure 22 indicate that the DIR and OE pins must be LOW (0V or GND).

DIR (pin 1, upper left) can be seen to connect on the schematic (via pathway "11" and demonstrated by following the PCB trace and proven by continuity check with a voltmeter) to header pin P4-3.

OE (pin 19, second right) connects (via pathway "10") to header pin P1-2.
These pins are shown connected by grey and white jumpers to Raspbery Pi GPIO pins 10 and 12.

**However, unless there is a script running on the Pi to cause these pins to go LOW, they will "float" and be neither HIGH nor LOW preventing the chip from functioning properly. There is no mention of running a script on the pi for this test. Instead, we connected them to two of many spare GND pins on the RPi such as physical pins 9 and 14 to force them LOW.**

+5V (P1-1) red wire to RPi +5V (pin 2). Check.

GND (P4-4) black wire to RPi GND (pin 6). Check.

During testing at each step the +3.3V purple wire to RPi +3.3V (pin 1) needs to march down the logic shifter headers P1-3 through P4-2. At each step confirm the +3.3V on the corresponding Bx pin on the right side of the shifter (according to the schematic) and look for the +5V on its partner Ax on the left side one pin up.

title: Kill Switch
text:
Kill Switch
Kill Switch:
It is my firm belief that, just as NASA has a Range Safety Officer whose job it is to abort a mission should the missile veer off course, every test of a robot of more than trivial power needs a Robot Safety Officer whose job it is to stop the robot should it behave in unintended ways. To this effect we installed a "kill switch", a keychain remote controlled power switch. We placed it between the voltmeter and the RoboClaw power tree while allowing unimpeded power take-off to the 5V regulator and thus to the brains of the robot. In addition to the main power switch, the RSO must activate the remote to permit power to the motors. Another push of the remote button stops the rover in its tracks. The one pictured was obtained long ago from a forgotten source. A Google of "keychain remote" will reveal many similar. The photo also reveals two other modifications made to the laser-cut acrylic back plate. One was for the power switch which was awkward to place elsewhere on the body. Two additional holes permitted passage of the battery connectors which don't fit the 1/2" holes in the aluminum pattern plates. Future modification plans are to replace the power toggle switch with an illuminated button switch, the better to indicate the power status & facilitate emergency shut-off.

title: Decoupling capacitors on opamps
text:
Decoupling capacitors on opamps
A decoupling capacitor (say 100nF) should be provided at the Vcc pin on each of the voltage-follower opamps in the encoder system. Given the use of long wires and amateur construction with DuPont jumper wires, parasitic inductance in the 5V supply wires is likely to be significant, and the proper use of decoupling capacitors at each IC is universally good practice.

The master BOM says that 4x LM358 are used - but is this correct?
There are 4 encoder channels, so 2 LM358s should be needed. (They are a dual opamp.)
In fact, a single quad opamp could be used (eg. LM324) meaning one less part.

15kΩ : 10kΩ would provide the most correct voltage division of 5V to 2V, assuming zero output impedance in the encoder, and remains a common E12 value.

Wouldn't choosing an encoder with TTL quadrature output and connecting this to the motor drive board completely eliminate the need for this circuit, instead of purchasing encoders with the analog output option?

B7 wheel mounting screw 1.25" is too long. Use 5/8" (or 3/4")

This goes way back to the initial build but I don't see it addressed elsewhere.
The BOM & directions call for B7 6-32 x 1 1/4" screws to mount the wheels on the drive motor shaft clamp hub. This gives extra room to see where the screws are going as you're kind of screwing blind into the hub. However, even before being fully inserted the screws strike the motor and prevent rotation and the screw going all the way in. The clamp hub can be installed two ways and the build doesn't specify and has images showing it both ways - with the round part toward the wheel or toward the motor. If installed toward the motor a 3/4" screw works ok. If installed toward the wheel, the hub recesses into the wheel a little more so you need a 5/8" screw to prevent locking.

I re-discovered this after partly dis-assembling the rover for the new control board. I had put off applying Loctite to the rover not being sure how often I might have to rework parts of it. Now that the mechanics seem stable, I took the opportunity to apply it. I re-mounted all the hubs with the round part out. Not sure how they were mounted before, prob inward as I found that I could hand-turn the motor (to be sure I hadn't epoxied it to the hub) with the hub alone, but not with the wheel attached using 3/4" screws. Now I've got to replace my 3/4" screws w/ 5/8". The original discovery was before I learned how to post to Github and Tapatalk forums.

Jim Phel

title: JST KR Arduino Shield J5 to Control Board J10 backwards/inconsistent
text:
JST KR Arduino Shield J5 to Control Board J10 backwards/inconsistent
Noticed an inconsistency with Arduino Shield connector J5, which connects to mainboard.

In Figure 17 and in the assembly text, notch for this connector is to face OUTWARDS. 

Later in the same document, Figure 31 shows the opposite. Where the notch faces INWARDS.

Which is correct? Both!

Figure 17 (face OUTWARDS) is consistent with JST-KR connector specification for pin 1 to line up with pin 1 in schematic. (Carries +12V) It also matches the alignment for the connector on main board.

However, the cable on the parts list Digi-Key 455-3156-ND is wired such that pin 1 on one side is pin 6 on the other. (pin 2 on one is pin 5 on other, etc.) Meaning the circuit is won't work unless the Arduino shield connector is flipped around [Figure 31]. (Or flip the main board connector, but obviously not both.)

Suggested action:
* Keep pins aligned as per JST-KR specification, with pin 1 representing +12V, on both Arduino shield and main board. (Figure 17 is correct, Figure 31 is wrong.)
* Replace cable 455-3156-ND with Digi-Key 455-3144-ND which is "reversed" so pin 1 on one connector matches with pin 1 on the other connector.

title: Main PCB: Potential collision RoboClaw 1 and C2
text:
Main PCB: Potential collision RoboClaw 1 and C2
Using mainboard Rev E.

Our five RoboClaw controllers are mounted with the tops of their electrolytic capacitors flush against the main board. On RoboClaw 2-5, they meet up with flat uninterrupted PCB. In Rev E, however, capacitor C2 is directly on the other side of RoboClaw 1's capacitors. Its soldering points can barely clear in between two capacitor cans of RoboClaw 1. And this is when trimmed back almost flush.

If someone has a large solder joint that hasn't been trimmed, doesn't notice the potential for collision, and crank the screws tight while installing their RoboClaw 1, they risk puncturing the electrolytics.

Consider moving C2 to reduce the chance for this potential problem.

title: Electrical Build doc: Inconsistent wire gauge X1, X2. 16 or 20 AWG?

Electrical Build doc: Inconsistent wire gauge X1, X2. 16 or 20 AWG?
In Electrical Build.pdf:

Table 1 parts to build battery connector lists X1 (red) and X2 (black) as 16 AWG wires.

Table 3 in the same document lists X1 and X2 as 20 AWG wires.

Parts list describe X1/X2 as 20 AWG wires and that's what I purchased.

If table 1 is incorrect and we're supposed to use 20 AWG wires for battery, the typical guidance for wires recommend not to exceed 5A for 20 AWG. 20 AWG wires may burn up before tripping the 10A fuse.

If table 1 is correct and Table 3+parts list is wrong, 16 AWG is awfully thick to route through rover suspension for motors.

Perhaps the wires of table 1 and 3 are intended to be different wires of different gauge?

title: Rover 6" PVC Neck Too Long For Cable E26
text:
Rover 6" PVC Neck Too Long For Cable E26
(Related issue: #168) 

Head Assembly Build PDF, section 3.1:

> You can make your rover's neck as long as you'd like, but for reference we cut our "neck" PVC pipe to be roughly 6 inches long.

The neck is actually constrained by the length of cable (E26) connecting main board to Arduino shield, which is 12 inches (~300mm) long.

In the first iteration I cut a 7-inch long PVC pipe. I found the cable could not reach its connector.

 

With a 5 inch (~128 cm) length of pipe, the cable could reach, but only barely which places a lot of stress on cable and connectors.

It is far better to cut PVC down to 4.5 inch (~115mm) for some slack and reduce tension.

 

Alternate solution: order a longer cable E26. See also related issue #168

title: Corner Steering Angle Calculation Inconsistent With PCB Rev E
text:
Corner Steering Angle Calculation Inconsistent With PCB Rev E
RE: Steering angle calculation in file ```Software\rover-code\ROS\osr\scripts\robot.py``` method ```calculateTargetDeg(self, radius)```

This calculation is based on RoboClaw 4 M1 steering the front left wheel, 4M2 steers back left. And RoboClaw 5M1 steeris back right, 5M2 steers front right. This is consistent with Electrical Build PDF Figure 9 (See also issue #174 ) but inconsistent with PCB Rev E which is left-right reversed for the two RoboClaws.

## Symptom:

The calculated Ackermann angles are left/right reversed, causing inside and outside steering wheels to fight each other instead of turning in a coordinated fashion.

## Workaround:

Assign angles according to PCB Rev E locations, which means swapping 1234 to 4321.

Edit lines 126-129 from
```
 ang1 = int(math.degrees(math.atan(self.d1/(abs(r)+self.d3))))
 ang2 = int(math.degrees(math.atan(self.d2/(abs(r)+self.d3))))
 ang3 = int(math.degrees(math.atan(self.d2/(abs(r)-self.d3))))
 ang4 = int(math.degrees(math.atan(self.d1/(abs(r)-self.d3))))
```

To
```
 ang4 = int(math.degrees(math.atan(self.d1/(abs(r)+self.d3))))
 ang3 = int(math.degrees(math.atan(self.d2/(abs(r)+self.d3))))
 ang2 = int(math.degrees(math.atan(self.d2/(abs(r)-self.d3))))
 ang1 = int(math.degrees(math.atan(self.d1/(abs(r)-self.d3))))
```

Alternate workaround: Same mathematical results can be obtained by reversing addition/subtraction of ```self.d3``` instead of changing variable assignment.

title: Wheel Velocity Calculation Left/Right Reversed
text:
Wheel Velocity Calculation Left/Right Reversed
RE: Steering angle calculation in file ```Software\rover-code\ROS\osr\scripts\robot.py``` method ```calculateVelocity(self,v,r)```

When turning, the commanded wheel velocities are reversed from what they should be: inside wheels are commanded to turn faster than outside wheels. This may be a consequence of multiple issues upstream (See #174, #175 ) and not necessarily a bug in this math.

## Symptom: 
Depending on traction conditions, one of two things happen during a turn:
1. Rover speed dictated by the slow outer wheels. Inner wheels are scrubbing against the ground, slipping faster than their surface velocity.
OR
2. Rover speed dictated by the faster inner wheels. Outer wheels skid on the surface, turning slower than their surface velocity.

## Workaround:
Reverse the velocity assignment for turning radius greater/less than zero;

Edit lines 105-108 From
```
 if (r 0):
 velocity = [v6,v5,v4,v3,v2,v1]
```

To
```
 if (r > 0):
 velocity = [v1,v2,v3,v4,v5,v6]
 elif (r < 0):
 velocity = [v6,v5,v4,v3,v2,v1]
```

title: PCB Rev E no electrical continuity between J6, J7 for pin 16 and all grounds
text:
PCB Rev E no electrical continuity between J6, J7 for pin 16 and all grounds
### Pin 16 ###

AllPCB brought up a problem with rover PCB rev E: there is a partial traces to connect pin 16 on J6 (Raspberry Pi GPIO in) to its counterpart on J7 (Raspberry Pi GPIO out). However, it is incomplete so there would be no electrical connection. (Their diagram suggests a via at the location of the blue dot, but that would connect pin 13 to pin 16 which is not what we want.)

 

After this was brought up, testing with meter on a PCB made by JLCPCB confirmed the lack of continuity.

Current workaround: ignore the flaw and proceed, because J7 is unused.

But this will impede ability to extend the rover beyond JPL spec, a flawed J7 means modifications that need pin 16 would not be able to easily tap into Raspberry PI GPIO. Until this is addressed, using pin 16 will involve soldering to the back of J6 with fine wire and a steady hand.

### Ground ###

In addition to pin 16, testing with a continuity meter indicates all the GPIO ground pins are connected to PCB ground plane on J7 (RPI_GPIO OUT) but left floating on J6 (RPIGPIO_IN).

title: Orientation of wheel clamping hub S14A is important and should be clarified and depicted consistently
text:
Orientation of wheel clamping hub S14A is important and should be clarified and depicted consistently
RE: Wheel Assembly Build Doc PDF

Clamping hub S14A is flat on one side and the other side has a cylindrical protrusion. Diameter of this cylinder is smaller than wheel center, meaning it easily fits inside the wheel which will bolt against the surface of four tapped holes of S14A. As a result, the location of this wheel mating surface would vary by a few millimeters depending on whether S14A is bolted flat-side-in or flat-side-out. Both were depicted in documentation (list below.)

When bolted flat-side-in, with certain Traxxas wheels their mounting screw B5 extends far enough past hub S14A to make contact with face of motor E45 gearbox. In case of light contact, they will acts as brake pads. In case of strong contact, they will prevent the wheel from turning.

If this situation is not detected before motor calibration begins, applying motor power will strip gears in the gearbox.

Recommendation: Make all diagrams consistently flat-side-out and caution rover builders to examine their wheel mounting bolts to ensure their wheels can turn before applying motor power.

In Wheel Assembly Build PDF as of late August 2019:

_Figure 1: Drilling the Wheels_ shows flat side in
_Figure 3: Wheel Step 1_ shows flat side out
_Figure 4: Wheel Step 2_ shows flat side in

title: Feedback: 30AWG wire (X3, X4, X5, X6) too difficult to work with.
text:
Feedback: 30AWG wire (X3, X4, X5, X6) too difficult to work with.
As of August 2019, the wires for carrying wheel drive motor encoder data were 30AWG wires. For disambiguation there were four colors (X3 through X6). They are intended to connect to side-entry terminal blocks E3 on rover PCB.

Their small diameter are useful for routing through small gaps, helped by the flexible insulator. However, when trying to insert bare wires into E3, their small size is easily bent out of position. Once in position, they are so thin the screw-down terminal can't make solid contact, leading to electrical gremlins and/or wires falling out.

Akin's Australia and US rover build teams both independently came to the same conclusion these wire needed larger and more durable ends. (We didn't realize this until weeks after the fact.) The Australian rover got soldered headers, the USA rover received crimped-on connectors.

__Low-impact solution:__
Switch X3 - X6 to larger diameter wires.

__High-impact solution:__
For a future PCB revision, switch from side-entry terminal blocks to commodity wire-to-board electrical connectors. (JST-XH or similar.) It will require more up-front work to wire up the connector, though note in this case we ended up doing similar work anyway. The payoff is ease of disassembly for diagnosis and repair. For each wheel, one single plug by hand versus 6 individual wires and screwdrivers.

(Or do both: larger diameter wires AND wire-to-board connectors)

title: PCB fragile traces
text:
PCB fragile traces
Having recently upgraded the 4 steering motors to the new specs and all 6 drive motors to the REV Robotics HEX motors I re-tuned them all using Basicmicro Motion Studio and they checked out ok (after I fixed a couple Molex connections that came loose.) But when I tested it with the Xbox controller, the left side steering was paralyzed. Logic demanded that it was a problem between the Pi and the RoboClaws. Continuity check between the Pi and the PCB was intact. Since communication with the RCs through the PCB was serial, there had to be a problem near RC5/132 that controlled steering motors 3 and 4. [BTW, Section 4.2 figure 9 seems mis-labeled to me. Front/Back are reversed and the steering motors are switched right/left when viewed from above.] Examining the PCB I found a blown trace near RC5. Above RC5 and next to RC3 in attached pic. The two red wires near the fried trace are jumpers from a previous blown trace to the LED display. The second pic shows the repair (prior to cleaning up the flux and solder stains). Looking at the Gerber of the PCB (I have Rev D. Not sure what the changes are to the current Rev E) it seems that the traces are very narrow and wouldn't be able to handle much current making them more susceptible to failure. Would suggest increasing the width of all traces as much as possible on any future revision. (along with a number of other changes, but that's a different story.)

title: Max current for roboclaws should be set at 15A
text:

When that current is set to a value that is too low, weird stuff starts to happen (MBH error gets triggered). The roboclaw protects itself from overcurrent regardless of that setting.

title: Add filter capacitors to quadrature encoder connections
text:
Add filter capacitors to quadrature encoder connections
The Servo City HD Premium Gear Motors with encoders have a capacitor acting as a snubber on the encoder board. This capacitor couples the 20kHz PWM voltage from the RoboClaws into the encoder signals. The 20kHz noise causes errors, showing up as extra pulses, when the RoboClaws read the encoders. BasicMicro recommends 0.01uF capacitors on the encoder lines to filter out the 20kHz noise. Locations for these capacitors need to be added to the control PCB. 

The snubber circuit is a poor design that supposedly shows up in similar motors that have built-in encoders. The extra capacitors can be considered optional for motors that do not need them, but adding the filtering should not impact motors that do not need them, and the extra filtering is not a bad idea.

The 0.1uF capacitors already in use on the board are too large for this purpose and filter out the encoder signals entirely at high motor speeds. The 0.01uF capacitors eventually specified for the project should have a different form factor to keep them from getting mixed up with the 0.1uF capacitors.

title: Submodule paths are incorrect
text:
Submodule paths are incorrect
# Problem

The following commands fail to update the Git submodules:

```
git submodule init
git submodule update
```

After cloning the project with `git clone https://github.com/nasa-jpl/open-source-rover.git` we should have the directories that contain the submodules (`software/android-app`, and `software/rover-code`), but none of the files within.

Then `git submodule init` should initialize the local configuration file, and `git submodule update` should fetch the data from nasa-jpl/osr-android-app and nasa-jpl/osr-rover-code.

More information on Git submodules.

# Solution 1

1. Update paths in `.gitmodules`.
2. Commit the submodules.

# Solution 2

1. Remove the Git submodules.
2. Provide instructions on how to remove Git submodules from a local repo.

title: Add final newlines
text:
Add final newlines
Having a newline character at the end of a file prevents the following in diffs:

```
\ No newline at end of file
```

or in the GitLab GUI the last of the file appearing in the diff without being modified. As seen in `mechanical/wheel_assembly/README.md` in commit 3aa8686cbd4e0630ba8954e1dd65db4dbf2523f2:

```diff
- Congratulations, you finished another major assembly!
+ Congratulations, you finished another major assembly!
```

## 1. Add final newlines

Add final new lines to the following files:

* `DISCLAIMER.txt`
* `LICENSE.txt`
* `electrical/latex_docs/electrical_assembly/run_pdflatex.sh`
* `examples/README_example.md`
* `software/README.md`
* `software/latex_docs/software_controls/Software Controls.tex`


## 2. Add a `.editorconfig` file

To limit the future occurrences of files without a final newline, I propose adding an .editorconfig file to the repo with the following contents:

```ini
root = true

[*]
insert_final_newline = true
```

This will instruct editors to append a final newline to text files when they are saved.

`.editorconfig` is pre-installed on about 26 editors and plugins are available for another 20 or so editors.

For those who are not using a editor with `.editorconfig` support, `.editorconfig` will serve as a recommendation on how their editor should be manually configured.

title: `master_parts_list_raw.csv` has `crlf` line endings
text:
`master_parts_list_raw.csv` has `crlf` line endings
`master_parts_list_raw.csv` has `crlf` line endings. Contributors can inadvertently change the line endings for every line of the file when intending to edit only a few lines.

Two proposals to mitigate this are:

## Option 1 #312 superseded by b5295acc83eda2de8eafed4b60b9c0142b2d4c67

~~Specify in `.editorconfig` that `master_parts_list_raw.csv` has `crlf` line endings. Other files have `lf` line endings.~~

```ini
root = true

[*]
end_of_line = lf
insert_final_newline = true

[parts_list/master_parts_list_raw.csv]
end_of_line = crlf
```

_Originally posted by @sethfischer in https://github.com/nasa-jpl/open-source-rover/issues/298#issuecomment-853584639_

## Option 2 #320

Commit `master_parts_list_raw.csv` to the repo with Unix line endings and suggest contributors use Git's `core.autocrlf` setting.

The use of this setting could be documented in a file such as `.github/CONTRIBUTING.md` or `CONTRIBUTING.md`.

I believe option 2 would be a more typical approach when when contributors use a mix of operating systems.

title: Test point designation letter
text:
Test point designation letter
The designation letter for the control board PCB test points is "T" (T1-T20).

The parts list has references **T1**-**T11** which are spacers and threaded stand-offs.

To avoid ambiguity the test point designator prefix could be changed to "TP", which is recommended by *ASME Y14.44* and *IEEE Std 315* *Graphic Symbols for Electrical and Electronics Diagrams (Including Reference Designation Letters)*.

Implementing this change will also improve the relevance of search results when using GitHub search, or searching a local copy of the documentation.

### Notes

1. Other designation letters on the control board PCB are "J" (connectors), "C" (capacitors), and "R" (resistors). All of which comply with the suggestions in section 22.4 of *ASME Y14.44* and *IEEE Std 315*; and do not conflict with a part reference in `parts_list/master_parts_list_raw.csv`.
1. The designation letter "T" is suggested for transformers and coils.
1. Those who don't have access to *ASME Y14.44* or *IEEE Std 315* may refer to https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reference_designator.

title: Use relative paths for images

## Proposal

Make all image src links relative.

## Justification

Using relative links allows correct rendering of a local preview. For this reason GitHub's docs recommend using relative links:

> Relative links are easier for users who clone your repository. Absolute links may not work in clones of your repository - we recommend using relative links to refer to other files within your repository.

Being able to preview rendered Markdown before pushing is important as it can reduce the number of errors.

In `mechanical/head_assembly/README.md` there is one relative link, with the remaining being absolute.

Hello.

You have an Apache license that says that you can use and distribute the sources pretty much however you like. And then you also have a disclaimer that places many restrictions on usage and distribution (you have to be a certain age, you need another license to use this commercially, etc, etc). These two statements are incompatible. You should pick which terms you actually want to distribute this under, and then remove the other license statement. title: Git repo history is large, consider recommending --depth 1
text:
Git repo history is large, consider recommending --depth 1
When cloning the repo with

```
git clone https://github.com/nasa-jpl/open-source-rover.git
```

The resulting folder is 3.4GB, mostly under .git/objects:

```
$ du -hcd2 | sort -h
...
2.9G ./.git/objects
3.4G .
3.4G total
```

The size isn't a whole lot by today's standards but it took a while to clone the repo from github. 

After cloning it I tried a couple things to see if the size could be easily reduced. First I tried using `git gc --aggressive --prune` and then `git repack -a -d -f --depth=250 --window=250` but it was still around 3.4GB. I think it's just because of the long history with some large files. Most users will only need the most recent revisions so it'd be good to include something in the instructions or the contributions page like

```
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/nasa-jpl/open-source-rover.git
```

This doesn't pull the whole history with the repo but it gets all the current files. I think it's sufficient even for most contributors. The resulting directory has only 883M in it today, about half of that is under the `.git/` folder.

The wiring instructions require six 6-pin connectors made by Molex. The parts list currently lists only the mating part for the PCB - Molex 1726750613.

This came out of a thread on Slack. I'm working on a PR to update the relevant docs but I wanted to collect the info in one spot first.

### Parts

So I ordered some Molex 0469920610 housings and pins 0039000077 from Digikey. They seem to fit but I've only made one cable with them so far. I used the same crimp tool as I did for the DuPont and JST-XH connectors. It wasn't perfect but seems workable. The housings are black so I can't mark them following the instructions.

### Assembled alternative

There is also a pigtail cable assembly in various lengths. I ordered Molex 2153261063 which is 60cm long and uses 16 AWG wire. The assembly could be more convenient but: 1. the assemblies seem relatively expensive, 2. they're less available, and 3. the wire gauge seems like it might be too large for the DuPont pins.

To be explicit (so I don't have to look it up again) this connector housing is described by Molex as a Mini-Fit Jr. Receptacle Housing, Dual Row, Nylon 6/6, UL 94V-2, 6 Circuits, Glow-Wire Capable, Black from the series Mini-Fit Jr 46992. And the pins are Mini-Fit Jr. Overall Tin female crimp terminals from the series Mini-Fit Jr 5556.

Section 4.5 of PCB assembly instructions is a little confusing
While we were soldering the brainboard, section 4.5 was a bit confusing due to how the instructions were worded.

Originally, with the many reference to E-STOP and LED indicators, our eyes kept being drawn to T13, T14, T15, and we wondered what component was supposed to be installed there.

After much discussion among the group and rereading of the instructions, we believe section 4.5 was about installing the transistors (Q2-Q6) and the diodes (D8 and D9). And rereading the earlier instructions, we can see that other T* references were called test points.

So reasons we are confused:

In previous instructions, the bullets indicated the components (using their reference part number) to be installed, without a lot of verbiage. In section 4.5, there are a bunch of words about E-STOP and then the actual transistor part numbers. The diodes aren't even in the bullets but in a separate paragraph.

Additionally, since we are soldering the PCB over several weeks, we tend to focus on the section in front of us, and may not remember that you have been consistently using T* designators for test points. Anyone who takes the LED array part for U5 and U6 from the board, the schematic files, or the BOM's Digi-Key column is sent to DC7G3HWA, which Digi-Key lists as obsolete.

The BOM (row A37 of BOM/bom_v2.0.3_board_ref_parts.csv) already
names the current Kingbright part (DC10CGKWA), a note there says
DC7G3HWA was the v2.0.1 part and is now obsolete. The order export
BOM/digikey_bom_4-20-2023.csv shows DC10CGKWA (754-2186-ND) as what
was bought. But Control_Boards.kicad_pcb and the placed symbols in
Motor_Board.kicad_sch (U5) and Brain_Board.kicad_sch (U6) still
carry DC7G3HWA as the Value, and row A37's Digi-Key Part cell still
reads DC7G3HWA instead of a SKU.

The fix: set the U5/U6 Value to DC10CGKWA in the
layout and the two placed symbols, and set A37's Digi-Key Part cell
to 754-2186-ND.

To see it:

 grep -n '"Value" "DC7G3HWA"' electrical/pcb/control_board/Control_Boards.kicad_pcb electrical/pcb/control_board/Motor_Board.kicad_sch electrical/pcb/control_board/Brain_Board.kicad_sch
 grep -n 'DC10CGKWA\|DC7G3HWA' electrical/pcb/control_board/BOM/bom_v2.0.3_board_ref_parts.csv

second is the placed symbol.
